Lesson 10 · Decide where to expand

Difference-in-differences and panel data

We have evaluated a randomized pilot and a voluntary cohort. The final study follows another set of stores as the policy expands, using their earlier outcomes to construct the comparison.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

The chain introduces alerts at 25 of its 50 remaining stores in week 25. These stores began with higher stockout rates. How much of their later improvement came from alerts, beyond the movement already occurring elsewhere? Learn how comparing changes constructs the missing no-alert path, then trace the result from weekly records to the final expansion decision.

Separate persistent differences from changes over time

General theory

A before-and-after improvement includes both treatment and background movement

  • D=1: units treated after the intervention date
  • D=0: comparison units remaining untreated
  • Before and after use the same outcome definition
  • A panel follows the same units in both periods

A policy can begin while demand, seasonality or operations are already changing. Comparing a treated group with its own past removes persistent differences across units, but still includes these time changes. A comparison group supplies a candidate estimate of the background movement. This lesson uses a balanced panel with one common intervention date; define the groups and windows before computing an effect.

Two subtractions remove the group level and the common time change

Additive mean model: b is a persistent level gap; c is a shared change
Group meanBeforeAfterChange
Comparisonaa+cc
Treateda+ba+b+c+τc+τ
Treated − comparisonbb+ττ

Read the last column first: differencing within each group removes its starting level. Then subtract the comparison change from the treated change, leaving τ. Reading across the last row gives the same result. This table expresses a population mean model with a common untreated change; observed sample means also contain sampling variation. It does not claim that every unit’s residual cancels exactly.

The conventional DiD is the treated change minus the comparison change

DiD=(Y¯1,after−Y¯1,before)−(Y¯0,after−Y¯0,before)

The subscripts 1 and 0 label treatment groups, not time. A negative DiD means the outcome fell more, or rose less, in the treated group. Whether that is favorable depends on the outcome: fewer stockouts are desirable. Keep the conventional signed outcome effect in the theory and explicitly reverse its sign when reporting a positive reduction in the application.

Identify the missing untreated change for the treated population

General theory

Potential outcomes reveal the comparison that the data cannot show

ATT=E[Yafter(1)−Yafter(0)∣D=1]Missing: E[Yafter(0)∣D=1]

ATT is the average treatment effect on the treated group. Yafter(1) and Yafter(0) describe the same unit with and without treatment after the intervention. We observe only the option received. No anticipation lets the baseline outcome represent the untreated state for future adopters; consistency links received treatment to the observed outcome, and the comparison group must remain untreated by this intervention, including spillovers.

The observed difference in changes equals ATT plus untreated-trend bias

DiD=ATT+δδ=E[ΔY(0)∣D=1]−E[ΔY(0)∣D=0]

Start with the treated group’s observed change, E[Yafter(1)−Ybefore(0)|D=1]. Add and subtract its missing Yafter(0). The expression becomes its treatment effect plus its untreated change. Subtracting the comparison group’s untreated change leaves ATT plus δ. The appendix writes every step. The extra term shows precisely what remains when the untreated trends differ.

Parallel trends sets the remaining bias term to zero

E[ΔY(0)∣D=1]=E[ΔY(0)∣D=0]δ=0⟹DiD=ATT

Parallel trends concerns average changes without treatment, not equal starting levels or identical observed paths after treatment. A persistent level gap is compatible with this condition. The operating history and pre-period evidence help assess the comparison; they do not make the missing after-period path observable. Selected adopters can have different treatment effects from other stores, so an ATT does not automatically become an all-store ATE.

Express the same contrast through two fitted equations

General theory

The group-by-period interaction recovers the four-cell contrast

Yit=a+bDi+cAftert+d(Di×Aftert)+eit

The intercept is the comparison mean before treatment. b is the initial group gap; c is the comparison change; d is the additional treated change. The four combinations of D and After give four fitted means. On the same observations and weights, this saturated two-by-two model reproduces the difference of changes exactly. Identification still comes from the trend argument, not from fitting an interaction.

First differences remove a unit’s persistent level and leave one change

ΔYi=α+βDi+uiα=comparison change;β=signed DiD

With two periods and complete paired observations, subtract before from after within each unit. A time-invariant unit component disappears. Regressing those changes on an intercept and D estimates the difference between the two group mean changes. Under the common balanced design, the first-difference and interaction coefficients agree. Preserve the unit in the uncertainty calculation rather than treating repeated rows as independent assignments.

Controls and weights answer specified questions about changes and populations

  • Baseline controls allow changes to vary with starting conditions
  • Subgroups restrict the population being compared
  • Fixed baseline weights change which units count most
  • Keep sample, target and specification beside every estimate

Adjustment is useful when untreated changes differ systematically with measured starting conditions and a conditional trend argument is credible. Choose controls by timing and causal role, using Lesson 8’s logic; being measured early does not make every variable a suitable control. Priority or exposure weights define a target average. Inverse-variance weights instead address error precision under an explicit error model.

Connect the foundations before calculating

General theory

Store and time effects extend the two-period comparison

Yit=αi+λt+τ[Di×1(t=final)]+uit

With a common treatment start, αᵢ represents stable store-level differences and λₜ the shared change at each date. Before estimating τ, explain why treated and comparison stores would share untreated changes. In a three-period illustration, store baselines are 10,12,14,16, every period adds 2 points, and the final-period treatment subtracts 3; the fitted coefficient recovers −3. Stable fixed effects cannot remove an unequal evolving shock. Staggered timing and varying treatment effects require further methods, left as an extension.

Build one complete change for each rollout store

Worked application

Eight hundred weekly records become fifty complete store changes

No store is excluded from this balanced rollout panel
StepRows / unitsDefinition
Keep S101–S150, weeks 17–32800 weekly rows50 stores × 16 weeks
Average within store and period100 period rows8 weeks before; 8 after
Pair by store ID and subtract50 changesAfter − before
Split by future adoption25 + 25 storesFixed group membership

The before window is weeks 17–24; the after window is weeks 25–32. Every week has 140 monitored product-days, so averaging weekly percentages gives the same rate as pooling the counts within a store-period. Equal windows also keep each store equally weighted. The lab checks a unique store-week key, eight weeks per window, complete pairs and one-to-one joins to baseline attributes.

Group membership exists before treatment becomes active

D is the offer field; active equals D×After in this window
Store group / periodDAfterD×After
Comparison, before000
Adopter, before100
Comparison, after010
Adopter, after111

A future adopter has D=1 in both periods. Coding D as zero before rollout would confuse group membership with active treatment and remove the initial group-gap term from the intended model. The cohort’s offer flag is constant within store. The active field switches on in week 25 for adopters and remains zero for comparisons.

Each store’s two averages produce the change used by the analysis

First five paired stores; changes are percentage points
StoreDBefore %After %Change
S101113.0410.18-2.86

For S101, 10.178571−13.035714=−2.857143 points. S103 is a comparison store and also improves, illustrating why an individual before-after change cannot isolate the policy effect. The group analysis uses all fifty changes. A missing period would prevent that unit from supplying a paired change and would require an explicit eligibility decision.

Locate the intervention in the observed history

Worked application

The rollout begins at week twenty-five after distinct starting levels

The selected adopters began with higher baseline stockout rates. The chart supplies context for the dated comparison and shows that the groups need not have the same level. The main estimate averages weeks 17–24 and 25–32; the earlier weeks help describe the history. Inspect other changes at the rollout date with the operations team. The complete thirty-two-week table is available in the appendix.

Construct the missing no-alert benchmark from four means

Worked application

Comparison stores worsen while adopter stores improve

Mean of twenty-five store outcomes per group and period
GroupBefore %After %Change
Adopters13.7310.39-3.35
Comparisons10.3611.601.24

The adopter change is −3.346429 points and the comparison change is +1.239286. The latter supplies the estimated background movement. Each cell uses the same stores with the same equal weights, so the change in group means equals the mean of within-store changes. This sample consistency is what lets the table and the regressions agree.

Subtracting the background change gives a 4.59-point stockout reduction

Signed DiD=−3.346429−1.239286=−4.585714Reported reduction=−DiD=4.585714 pointsNo-alert benchmark=13.732143+1.239286=14.971429%

A smaller stockout outcome is favorable, so the business result reports the negative of the conventional DiD. Under parallel trends, adopters would have moved from 13.73% to 14.97% without alerts. Their observed after mean is 10.39%. The estimated improvement attributable to the policy comparison is therefore larger than the adopter group’s raw 3.35-point improvement.

The dashed no-alert path makes the missing comparison visible

The dashed line is an inferred counterfactual, not an observed third group. It starts at the adopters’ own before mean and adds the comparison change. The vertical difference at the after period is the positive reduction. The lines connect period averages and should not be read as weekly trajectories. Their role is to make the identification argument and the subtraction concrete.

Recover the same result through regression

Worked application

Four fitted coefficients reconstruct the entire before-and-after table

Y = a + bD + cAfter + d(D×After)
CoefficientValueMeaning
a10.357143Comparison before mean
b3.375000Initial adopter gap
c1.239286Comparison change
d-4.585714Additional adopter change

These coefficients come from the one hundred store-period rows. For example, b=13.732143−10.357143=3.375. The intervention coefficient d is negative because the outcome is a stockout percentage. Its negative is the reported positive reduction. Retain all four terms when reconstructing the group-period predictions.

Substituting each indicator combination recovers its observed cell mean

The saturated regression reproduces all four equally weighted means
CellFitted sumPredicted %
Comparison beforea10.357143
Adopter beforea+b13.732143
Comparison aftera+c11.596429
Adopter aftera+b+c+d10.385714

The adopter-after cell needs every term: 10.357143 + 3.375 + 1.239286 − 4.585714 = 10.385714. These fitted cell means are exactly the sample group-period averages apart from rounding. This is an algebraic property of the saturated model. It does not establish the causal interpretation, which still depends on the untreated-trend comparison.

Regressing fifty store changes produces the same signed effect

ΔY^=1.239286−4.585714DD=0: +1.239286;D=1: −3.346429

The fifty-row change model and the one-hundred-row interaction model agree on the point estimate because they use the same balanced stores and weights. The former makes the independent unit visible. It also gives a natural place to add baseline characteristics when modeling differences in changes. Their uncertainty calculations must account for the respective row structure.

Use stores as the units of uncertainty

Worked application

Variation across fifty store changes gives the 3.92–5.25 interval

SE=scomparison225+sadopter225=0.3317895% interval=4.58571±2.0116×0.33178=[3.91830,5.25313] percentage points

Each group variance describes twenty-five independent store changes. Welch’s degrees of freedom are 47.107, giving the displayed t multiplier. Aggregating within store keeps the repeated weeks together. One hundred period rows do not mean one hundred independent stores. In a period-row regression, clustering by store preserves dependence; its finite-sample correction can produce a slightly different standard error. The appendix calculates both.

Check the comparison and show the adjusted result

Worked application

A pre-period placebo compares two windows before alerts began

Early: weeks 17–20; later: weeks 21–24Placebo reduction=−0.13571 points95% interval=[−1.39189,1.12047]

Repeat the same comparison of changes before any rollout treatment is active. The estimated divergence is small relative to its uncertainty. This is useful evidence about the chosen comparison, but the interval also allows nontrivial pre-period differences. Combine the diagnostic with knowledge of simultaneous changes; a test that does not reject is not a certificate for the unobserved post-period trend.

Baseline adjustment asks whether starting conditions explain different changes

ΔY=α+βD+γL+ηU+κB+uAdjusted reduction −β=4.00 points95% HC1 normal interval=[2.66,5.34]

L is delivery lead time, U is urban location and B is baseline stockout percentage measured in weeks 1–8. The model uses the same fifty store changes. Its constant β describes an additive adjusted group contrast; interpreting it causally requires a suitable conditional trend argument, overlap and specification. Do not choose between the adjusted 4.00 and unadjusted 4.59 merely because one is more attractive. The appendix shows the complete fitted coefficients.

Subgroup effects remain attached to their smaller comparison samples

Separate equal-store comparisons; percentage points
LocationAdoptersComparisonsReduction95% interval
Other9194.453.50–5.40
Urban1664.773.05–6.49

Urban stores have a somewhat larger estimated reduction, but only six urban comparison stores supply their background change. Compare both sample sizes and uncertainty. The two group estimates answer narrower population questions. A difference between their individual significance labels would not test whether the subgroup effects differ.

Make the weighting target visible before fitting weighted least squares

Worked application

Doubling long-lead stores creates an explicit planning-weighted comparison

Weight 2 if baseline lead time is at least four days; otherwise weight 1
GroupSum of weightsSum of weighted changesWeighted change
Comparison3441.964291.23424
Adopter48-160.89286-3.35193

Use each store’s fixed baseline weight in both periods. Divide the weighted sum of changes by the group’s weight total, not by its number of stores. The totals are 34 for comparisons and 48 for adopters. These priorities deliberately change how stores contribute. They are not measured sales counts or inverse estimates of error variance.

Weighted least squares reproduces the weighted difference in changes

Weighted mean change=∑iwiΔYi∑iwiWeighted reduction=1.234244−(−3.351935)=4.586178 points

Weighted least squares on an intercept and D gives the two weighted group means, so its treatment coefficient is their signed difference. The near equality to the unweighted 4.585714 is a result of these data and this priority rule, not a general identity. To interpret the new comparison causally, defend the untreated trend for the weighted target. Equal monitoring exposure explains why equal-store and exposure weighting coincide in the original analysis.

Translate differential-trend bias into the spending decision

Worked application

An unrelated favorable adopter shock would inflate the reported reduction

s=separate favorable adopter change in pointsReduction attributable to alerts=4.585714−sAccounting saving=8.4(4.585714−s)−20

This is a hypothetical sensitivity scenario. A separate favorable change makes the signed untreated-trend bias δ negative and the reported positive reduction too large. For example, s=1 point reduces the policy contrast to 3.585714 and the weekly saving to 10.12 currency units. An operational response caused by alerts belongs within their total effect; a genuinely unrelated simultaneous change is the concern in this exercise.

A 2.20-point unrelated improvement would erase the estimated accounting advantage

Break-even reduction=20140×0.01×6=2.380952Break-even shock=4.585714−2.380952=2.204762 points

A one-point stockout reduction avoids 1.4 stockout product-days per week; valued at 6 currency units each, it saves 8.4 before the 20-unit alert fee. The sensitivity threshold links the trend assumption to the decision. It is not an estimated shock, a confidence bound or a claim that such a shock occurred. It tells the director how large a competing explanation would need to be to remove the point estimate’s accounting gain.

Work through the reasoning gap

Worked application

Selecting temporarily high outcomes can create a false improvement

Both groups return to a common level; no store receives a treatment
Separate untreated scenarioBeforeAfterChange
Selected high stores1814-4
Comparison stores10144

The signed DiD is −4−4=−8, which would be reported as an 8-point reduction. The entire apparent effect comes from selecting groups during opposite temporary shocks. This is regression toward usual levels, not evidence that the actual rollout estimate is wrong. The exercise shows what its parallel-trend argument must rule out: investigate why high baseline stores were selected and use earlier histories to assess persistence.

Changing composition can reverse a reported time comparison

Each true change is −2; only A appears in the observed after export
Two stores in a separate exerciseBeforeAfter
Store A2018
Store B108, but missing from the export

The observed unpaired means give 18−15=+3, while the complete-pair change for A is −2. Neither automatically identifies the full-population effect: the paired analysis changes its target when B is missing. Report counts, IDs and missingness by group and date; compare complete-pair and defensible sensitivity results. A pre-trend test with a large p-value cannot prove future parallel trends, especially with low precision.

Complete the expansion recommendation with traceable evidence

Worked application

The rollout supports staged expansion for comparable stores with continued measurement

  • Later-adopter reduction: 4.59 points; interval 3.92–5.25
  • Accounting saving: 18.52 CU per adopter-week
  • Preserve dates, store IDs and the monitoring basket
  • Review simultaneous changes and the next target population

The saving interval is 12.91–24.13 currency units per adopter-week under the stated accounting rule. Continue staged expansion for stores resembling this cohort, documenting the next decision population. The final memo should bring together the earlier burden, forecasting work, randomized pilot, voluntary comparison and this rollout study. Each estimate has its own population and time window; the synthesis page assembles them without treating them as interchangeable measurements.

Explain, reconstruct, diagnose and transfer

Decision and synthesis

A nonsignificant pre-trend test cannot establish future parallel untreated trends

  • Calculate the false treatment effect after selecting temporarily high stores and compare paired versus unpaired changes.
  • A nonsignificant pre-trend test proves the future untreated trends are parallel. Explain why this does not follow.

Work independently or explain your reasoning to a partner. State the target, units and assumptions before calculating. The student notebook provides runnable setup and separate task cells; the companion solution checks the calculation. The lesson’s completed lab remains available as a reference, with its steps separated into smaller cells.

A credible rollout comparison checks timing, composition and competing shocks

  • Design a rollout evaluation with three baseline periods and a common start date. Explain store effects, time effects, a placebo, attrition checks and a competing-shock sensitivity.
  • Submit a calculation, an assumption and a justified next action

An acceptable answer can recommend more information, a narrower claim or no action. It must connect the method to the target and explain the consequence of a failed assumption. Use the assessment criteria after attempting the task; matching a supplied recommendation is not the grading objective.

After your attempt: check the reasoning

Open the assessment criteria

Recover false reduction 8, unpaired change +3 versus paired −2. The three-period illustration recovers −3. Fixed effects remove stable levels, not differential time-varying shocks.

Update the decision memo

The later rollout estimates a 4.59-point reduction for the selected adopters, with a 95% interval of 3.92–5.25 and an accounting saving of 18.52 CU per adopter-week. Continue staged expansion for comparable stores while recording timing and simultaneous changes. An unrelated favorable adopter shock of 2.20 points would erase the point estimate’s accounting advantage.

Make the call

Suppose a separate process change improved only adopter stores by one percentage point at rollout. What happens to the estimated alert reduction and accounting saving?

Compare your reasoning

Subtract that hypothetical one-point improvement: the alert reduction becomes 3.585714 points. Weekly accounting saving becomes 8.4×3.585714−20=10.12 CU. Distinguish a separate simultaneous cause from a mechanism that is itself caused by alerts.

The bigger picture

Difference-in-differences turns an operating history into an explicit missing comparison. The two subtractions remove persistent levels and a shared change; the untreated-trend argument gives the remaining contrast its causal meaning. Across business settings, keep the population, dates, unit and target weights visible from the raw records to the decision.

After your decision: open the known answer

The shared world’s expected reduction among the later adopters is 4.47 points. The time-comparison estimate is 4.59, reflecting the observed product-day outcomes in this realization.
